items.name: Survey
items.line: Measured, drawn and priced before anything starts.
about: We measure the house, read your architect's drawings and walk the job with you. Then we price it line by line, and you see every line.
Before anything is signed you have a fixed price and a programme for your house, week by week.

photo.alt: Hands with a pencil, scale rule and calculator over printed house plans on a desk

lines: Nothing changes at home. We visit to measure, and once more with your architect.

items.name: Structure
items.line: Foundations, steel and the dig, checked at every stage.
about: The groundworks, the footings and the slab, then the steel and the walls. Building control inspects at each stage, and so does your project manager.
This is the noisy part. We agree the hours with you and your neighbours before it starts.

photo.alt: Two-storey blockwork extension shell at the back of a brick house, wrapped in scaffolding

lines: The kitchen moves to a temporary one we set up in another room.
A dust wall and a zip door close off the back of the house.
The garden is a site; the side return is our way in.

items.name: Envelope
items.line: Roof, walls and glass. Dry from here.
about: The roof goes on, the glazing goes in and the house is weathertight. From here the work moves inside, and the garden starts to come back.

photo.alt: Timber-framed house with its roof trusses in place against a blue sky

lines: The house is weathertight again; the dust wall stays.
Deliveries of glass and roofing: we tell you the days.

items.name: Finish
items.line: Plaster, joinery and stone, then the snagging walk together.
about: First fix, plaster, then the joinery, stone and paint. The last two weeks are for the details nobody else would notice.
At handover we walk every room with you and write down anything that isn't right. Then we put it right.

photo.alt: Joiner's hands marking a timber board with a pencil among wood shavings

lines: Plasterers, then joiners and painters, room by room.
The new kitchen goes in; the temporary one goes out.
Water and power are off for a few hours on two or three days, always told a week ahead.

sections.title: The *contract*
text: We build on a fixed-price contract with a programme attached. If you change something, we price the change in writing before we do it.

sections.title: How you *pay*
text: In stages, as each one is finished and you have seen it. Never more than the work done so far.
We never change our bank details by email. Call us before paying if anything looks different.

sections.title: After *handover*
text: A twelve-month defects period, and a visit at six months to check the house has settled.

sections.title: Living at home *during the work*
text: Most of our clients stay in. We seal off the work, keep a kitchen running where we can, and tell you a week ahead about the noisy days and the ones when the water or power will be off.

items.name: Rear and side extensions
items.line: Kitchens that open to the garden, in brick, oak and glass.

photo.alt: Glazed garden-room extension on the side of an older house, set among trees and a lawn

includes: Party wall notices and building control handled with you
The kitchen fitted by our own joiners
about: Most of our work is a room at the back or side of a London house: a kitchen that opens to the garden, a little deeper than the old one, with light from above.
We build the extension and put the house back around it, so it looks as though it was always there. Try the size on your own kind of house on our 3D page.

items.name: Loft conversions
items.line: A bedroom and a bathroom under the roof.

photo.alt: Loft room under a pitched roof with a large roof window and a triangular gable window onto autumn trees, a white daybed and a wooden desk

includes: A dormer, a hip-to-gable or roof lights
A new staircase that matches the house
Insulation and fire protection to building regulations
about: A loft is the quickest way to a new bedroom without losing the garden. We build the dormer or the roof lights, the new stair, and a bathroom where the headroom allows.
Most of the work happens from the scaffold and the roof, so the house below carries on until we break through for the stair.

items.name: Basements
items.line: New rooms below the house, dry and full of light.

photo.alt: Bare concrete lower-ground room lit by daylight falling from a lightwell above a concrete stair

includes: Waterproofing, inspected before it is covered
about: A basement is careful work, done in a sequence the engineer sets and building control inspects. We dig in short sections and the house stays standing on solid ground the whole time.
We talk to your neighbours before we start, and keep talking.

items.name: Whole-house renovations
items.line: Houses stripped back and put right, room by room.

photo.alt: Oak-tread staircase with black metal balustrade in a bright white stairwell with framed pictures and pendant lights

about: Sometimes the house needs everything: the wiring, the heating, the floors and the walls, all at once. We take it back to the structure and build it up again in order.
Most families move out for the first part and back in for the finish. We plan that with you.

items.name: Kitchens and joinery

about: Our joiners make the kitchens, shelving, stairs and doors in our own workshop, and fit them themselves. The same hands that drew it at the bench set it level in your house.

journal.title: *Journal*
journal.intro: Notes from our projects: planning, building, and living through the work.

items.title: Planning a rear extension
items.author: Tom Pellow
items.summary: What decides how deep it can go, and the letter your neighbour needs.

photo.alt: Architectural drawing sheet showing elevations, a section and floor plans of a pitched-roof building

body: Most of the extensions we build start with one question: do we need planning permission? Often the answer is no, because many houses have permitted development rights. They come with limits, though, and a few of them decide the design.

The government's guidance says a single-storey rear extension can go out up to 3 metres from the original back wall of a terraced or semi-detached house, or 4 metres from a detached one, and be no more than 4 metres high. Under a separate process called prior approval, where your neighbours are consulted, those depths can be 6 and 8 metres.

Within 2 metres of the boundary, the eaves can be no higher than 3 metres. The materials should look similar to the house's. In a conservation area there are more limits: a side extension, for example, isn't permitted development there.

If we build on or at the boundary, work on a shared wall, or dig near your neighbour's foundations, the Party Wall Act applies, and you must give your neighbour notice between two months and a year before the work starts.
We check all of this at the survey, with your architect, before anything is drawn in detail. It's also why the model on our home page shows sizes, not promises.

items.title: Living through a renovation
items.author: Mei Lin
items.summary: Most of our clients stay at home. Here is how that works.

photo.alt: Long wooden dining table beside a pale kitchen wall, with a large window onto green hills

body: Staying at home while we work is possible for most extensions and many renovations. It takes planning, and it is easier when you know what each week will be like.

We seal the work off with a dust wall and a zip door, and keep a temporary kitchen running wherever we can. Every Friday you get a written update: what was done, a photograph, and what next week holds.

We tell you a week ahead about the noisy days, the deliveries that block the drive, and the mornings when the water or the power will be off. If a week is going to be hard, we say so, and some clients plan a few days away around it.

items.title: Choosing materials that last
items.author: Joe Hartley
items.summary: Oak, stone, lime and brass: why we keep coming back to them.

photo.alt: Fabric swatches, charcoal sketches and a glass vase arranged on a stone table

body: We use a short list of materials, and we use them again and again because we know how they age. Oak darkens. Honed limestone wears softly. Lime plaster lets an old wall breathe. Unlacquered brass takes on the hands that use it.
We put samples on your kitchen table before anything is ordered, and we leave them there for a week so you can see them in morning and evening light.

items.text: We stayed in the house the whole time. Every Friday there was a photo and a list for next week, and it was always right.
items.author: Clare H.

items.text: The price we signed was the price we paid, apart from the extra window we asked for, which they priced before they did it.
items.author: James and Ola K.

items.text: Mei sent the Friday update every single week, even the week nothing much happened. That's why we trusted the weeks when a lot did.
items.author: Priya and Tom S.

items.text: We were worried about the neighbours. They wrote to both sides before we'd even asked, and the party wall agreements came back within a fortnight.
items.author: Helen M.

items.text: The loft is the quietest room in the house. The joinery on the new stair is better than the original.
items.author: David R.

items.text: A little longer than the first programme because of what they found under the old floor, but they showed us, priced it, and we agreed before they carried on.
items.author: Anna and Joe L.

costs.title: What it *costs*
costs.intro: Every house is different, so we price yours line by line. Here is how, and what decides it.
how: We price from your architect's drawings and our own survey. You get a fixed price, line by line, so you can see what everything costs and change what you like before you sign.
If you change something once we've started, we price the change in writing before we do it. Nothing appears on an invoice that you haven't agreed.

drivers.name: Size and shape
drivers.line: Floor area matters, but so do corners, steps and how much of the old house we take down.

drivers.name: The ground
drivers.line: Soil, trees, drains and how deep the foundations need to go. We find out at the survey; a basement needs the engineer's investigation.

drivers.name: Steel and structure
drivers.line: Opening up the back of a house means steel beams and, sometimes, new foundations under the old walls.

drivers.name: Glass
drivers.line: Large sliding doors, roof lights and steel-framed screens are often the biggest single choice.

drivers.name: The finish
drivers.line: Floors, kitchen, stone and joinery. Our specification page shows what we usually use.

drivers.name: Access
drivers.line: A terrace with no side access means everything comes through the house. We plan for it, and it shows in the price.

separate.name: Structural engineer
separate.line: Calculations for the steel, the foundations and, for a basement, the whole sequence.

separate.name: Party wall surveyor

help: We check the rules for your house at the survey, with your architect. If an extension sits close to a limit, we suggest a lawful development certificate before we start, so everyone knows where they stand.
We draft party wall notices with you and send them early, because a neighbour who hears from us first is usually a neighbour who consents.

livingPage.intro: Most of our clients stay at home. Pick a start date and see what each stage is like.
tips: Plan a few days away for the noisiest week, if you can. We'll tell you which one it is.
Keep one room clean and closed: somewhere to sit at the end of the day.
Ask us to move the temporary kitchen near a window. You'll cook there for weeks.
Tell the neighbours yourself as well. A note from you goes further than our letter.
